title: Phrases, clauses and misplaced modifiers
keyIdea: A phrase is a group of words with no verb of its own; a clause has a verb. Many phrases and clauses are modifiers: they describe a noun (adjectival, telling which one) or a verb (adverbial, telling where, when or how). A modifier describes what it sits next to, so a misplaced one changes the meaning: "the dog in a tuxedo". An opening phrase describes the first noun after the comma, so "Covered in mud, Mum washed the dog" says Mum was muddy; that is a dangling modifier. Commas round a relative clause change its job: without them it picks out which ones, with them it adds a fact about all.
familyTip: Hunt for funny misplaced modifiers in signs and headlines, such as "Dog for sale: eats anything and loves children". Draw what the words literally say, then rewrite it. Ask: what does this phrase sit next to, and is that what it should describe?

visual.caption: Is the modifier next to the word it describes, or misplaced? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: The man in a tuxedo fed the dog.
The man fed the dog in a tuxedo.
Walking home, I saw a fox.
Walking home, the rain soaked me.
She served cake on paper plates to the children.
She served cake to the children on paper plates.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: link phrases to their words, act out a relative clause with and without commas, fix misplaced and dangling modifiers, and sort phrase jobs.

kid: A phrase is a group of words with no verb of its own, like "after lunch" or "with the red kite". A clause has a verb, like "who finished early".

Lots of phrases describe something. In "The girl with the red kite ran", the phrase tells you which girl. That job is adjectival. In "She ran across the field", the phrase tells you where she ran. That job is adverbial.

A phrase describes what it sits next to. "The man fed the dog in a tuxedo" puts the tuxedo on the dog. Move the phrase: "The man in a tuxedo fed the dog." An opening phrase describes the first noun after the comma. "Covered in mud, Mum washed the dog" says Mum is muddy. Write "Covered in mud, the dog was washed by Mum."
Commas matter too. "The students who finished early went outside" means only some went. "The students, who finished early, went outside" means all of them went, and all of them finished early.
adult: Ages 11 to 13. This is Common Core L.7.1a, explain the function of phrases and clauses in general and in specific sentences, and L.7.1c, place phrases and clauses within a sentence, recognising and correcting misplaced and dangling modifiers. It matches the Key Stage 3 grammar aims in the National Curriculum in England. Key words: phrase, clause, main clause, subordinate clause, relative clause, modifier, adjectival, adverbial, misplaced, dangling.

Form and function are different questions. A prepositional phrase such as "on the table" is adjectival in "the cup on the table is mine" and adverbial in "put the cup on the table". Ask what it tells you: which one, or where, when or how. A relative clause without commas is defining and picks out a subset; with commas it is non-defining and adds a fact about the whole group.

Common mistakes: reading a misplaced modifier the way the writer meant rather than the way the words say; fixing a dangling opener with a comma instead of naming the doer; judging a phrase by its first word rather than its job; and adding commas round a defining relative clause, which changes who is included. Be careful: the fix for a dangler is usually to put the real doer straight after the comma.

In the lab your child links three phrases to the word each describes. They act out a relative clause with and without commas and watch who walks outside. Then they slide a phrase until it sits by its noun, choose endings that fix dangling openers and sort one phrase type by its two jobs.

practice.prompt: In "The boy in the photo is my cousin", what job does "in the photo" do?
choices: Adjectival: it tells which boy
Adverbial: it tells where he is going
It is a main clause
practice.hint: Does the phrase pick out which boy, or tell you about an action?
practice.explain: It picks out which boy, so it does the job of an adjective. It has no verb, so it is a phrase, not a clause.

practice.prompt: A class has {n} pupils and {k} of them had a ticket. "The pupils who had a ticket got in." How many pupils got in?
practice.hint: With no commas, the clause picks out which pupils.
practice.explain: The clause "who had a ticket" picks out a group, so only those {k} pupils got in.

practice.prompt: Which sentence fixes "Running for the bus, my bag fell open"?
choices: Running for the bus, I felt my bag fall open.
Running for the bus my bag fell open.
My bag, running for the bus, fell open.
practice.hint: Who was really running? Put that person straight after the comma.
practice.explain: The opener describes the first noun after the comma, so it must be I, the person running, not the bag.

practice.prompt: A tray holds {n} cakes. "The cakes, which Mia baked, were sold." How many cakes were sold?
practice.hint: With commas, the clause just adds a fact. Does it pick out some cakes?
practice.explain: The commas make "which Mia baked" extra information about all the cakes, so all {n} were sold.

practice.prompt: Where should "with huge teeth" go in "I saw a shark on holiday"?
choices: Straight after "shark"
Straight after "holiday"
At the very start
practice.hint: What has the huge teeth? Put the phrase right next to it.
practice.explain: The shark has the teeth, so the phrase goes next to it: "On holiday, I saw a shark with huge teeth."

pool.prompt: "Covered in mud, Mum washed the dog." By the grammar, who is covered in mud?
choices: Mum
The dog
Nobody
pool.hint: Look at the first noun after the comma.
pool.explain: An opening phrase describes the first noun after the comma, so the sentence says Mum is muddy. That is a dangling modifier.

pool.prompt: Why is "before dawn" a phrase and not a clause?
choices: It has no verb
It is only two words
It comes at the end
pool.explain: A clause has a verb. "Before dawn" has none, so it is a phrase, whatever its length or place.

pool.prompt: In "We swam in the lake", what does "in the lake" describe?
choices: The verb swam: it tells where
The noun we: it tells which ones
Nothing: it is extra
pool.hint: Ask: where, when or how did something happen?
pool.explain: It tells where we swam, so it modifies the verb. That is an adverbial job.

pool.prompt: Which sentence has a misplaced modifier?
choices: The man fed the dog in a tuxedo.
The man in a tuxedo fed the dog.
In a tuxedo, the man fed the dog.
pool.hint: Which version puts the tuxedo next to the dog?
pool.explain: "the dog in a tuxedo" says the dog wears it. The other two put the phrase by the man.

pool.prompt: What do the commas do in "My sister, who lives in Leeds, is a nurse"?
choices: They add an extra fact about my sister
They pick out one sister from many
They join two main clauses
pool.hint: Is the clause needed to know which sister?
pool.explain: With commas the clause is extra information about my sister. Without them, it would pick out the sister who lives in Leeds from others.

pool.prompt: {n} dogs are in the park and {k} are barking. "The dogs that are barking belong to Jo." By this sentence, how many dogs belong to Jo?
pool.hint: A clause with no commas picks out which dogs.
pool.explain: "that are barking" picks out the {k} barking dogs, so {k} dogs belong to Jo.

pool.prompt: Which is the best fix for "After finishing my homework, the TV was switched on"?
choices: After finishing my homework, I switched on the TV.
After finishing my homework the TV was switched on.
The TV, after finishing my homework, was switched on.
pool.explain: I finished the homework, so I must come straight after the comma. Moving or dropping the comma does not fix it.

pool.prompt: A sentence has {a} adjectival phrases and {b} adverbial phrases. How many phrases describe a verb?
pool.hint: Adverbial phrases tell where, when or how about a verb.
pool.explain: Only the adverbial ones describe the verb, so {b} phrases do.

pool.prompt: "On the table" is adjectival in one sentence. Which?
choices: The cup on the table is mine.
Put the cup on the table.
She sat on the table.
pool.hint: Which one uses the phrase to tell you which cup?
pool.explain: In "the cup on the table is mine" it tells which cup. In the others it tells where something happens.
